Agentic trading and payments are emerging. AI lets retail process far more information, decide faster, and even build their own infrastructure for managing money.

AI has moved from capex build-out, to models, to execution. From here, the two cycles intertwine. The more of the world goes digital and the smarter agents get, the more crypto gets used. Compute markets running on crypto were named as a likely theme within the year.

So, where to position? Team execution matters more than ideas. We're looking at...

news.title:
ZEROBASE (@zerobasezk): MSCI’s decision to adopt new eligibility rules has injected fresh uncertainty into the already volatile world of cryptocurrency-related stocks, with Michael Saylor’s Strategy at the center of the discussion. On October 15 the index provider announced a framework that will treat certain companies as non-operating businesses and make them ineligible for its global equity benchmarks. 

The rules take effect at the close of November 30, and a final list of affected firms is scheduled for release on November 11. Strategy, the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, was flagged in earlier simulations alongside names such as Japan’s Metaplanet, raising the prospect that passive funds tracking MSCI indexes could be forced to sell billions of dollars’ worth of shares.

Analysts at JPMorgan have previously estimated that an exit could trigger roughly $2.8 billion in passive outflows for Strategy alone. The company has pushed back, arguing that the methodology is discriminatory against digital-asset treasury firms and that its software operations still make it an operating business. 

Existing constituents generally need to fail the screens across two consecutive annual reporting periods before removal, so any change is not instantaneous. Still, the prospect of index-driven selling adds pressure to the financing model that has allowed Strategy to keep accumulating Bitcoin through equity and preferred issuance.

As of mid-October Strategy holds 848,250 bitcoin, acquired at an average price near $75,444 for a total cost of about $64 billion. At recent market levels that stack is worth roughly $70 billion, leaving the position in paper profit. 

The company has continued modest purchases, adding 250 bitcoin in the latest reported period, while also managing a sizable cash reserve and repurchasing preferred shares. Its stock closed near $151 on October 15 after a 5.6 percent rebound, yet it remains well below the levels seen earlier in the cycle and continues to trade with extreme volatility that amplifies moves in Bitcoin itself.

Broader crypto-linked equities have shown similar choppiness. Coinbase, Circle, and various mining names have swung sharply alongside Bitcoin, which has hovered in the low-to-mid $80,000 range after stronger September performance. Inflation data and shifting expectations around monetary policy have contributed to the swings, with some names posting double-digit declines on individual days before recovering. 

Miners and pure treasury vehicles have often underperformed or outperformed Bitcoin depending on the week, while exchange and stablecoin-related stocks have reacted more to trading volumes and regulatory headlines.

The MSCI episode highlights a growing tension between traditional index construction and the rise of companies that treat Bitcoin as a core treasury asset rather than a secondary holding. Passive capital has become an important source of demand for these stocks; any sustained reduction in that bid could tighten the equity-issuance window that several of them rely on to fund further purchases. 

At the same time, Bitcoin’s price action and the companies’ own capital-management choices remain the dominant drivers. For investors the next several weeks will test how much weight the market assigns to the index risk versus the underlying digital-asset exposure that has defined these names for years.
